title: Live chat vs chatbot vs AI agent for B2B websites
summary: Live chat gives a reply, a chatbot gives a link, an AI agent gives the product. Storylane's guide to choosing for a B2B website, with data.
body_markdown:
Open the chat window on ten B2B websites and you will meet three different things wearing the same bubble. On one site a person types back. On another, three buttons appear and one of them leads to a form. On a third, something asks what you are trying to solve and then shows you the screen that solves it. Most teams choosing between them compare features when they should compare outcomes.


The choice gets simple with three questions. Who answers: a person, a script or an agent? When: business hours, always, or always? And what does the buyer walk away with: a reply, a link or the product? I call this the reply, link or product test, and it settles the live chat vs chatbot debate faster than any feature grid.


## What is the difference between live chat, a chatbot and an AI agent?


Live chat is a person on your team answering in a chat window. A chatbot is a script: it matches what the visitor typed to a rule or keyword and returns text, a link or a form. An AI agent is software that holds the conversation itself, trained on your material, and works toward a goal such as qualifying the visitor or booking a meeting.


The table puts the three questions side by side, plus staffing and cost.


Question Live chat Rule-based chatbot AI agent


Who answers A person on your team A script you wrote Software trained on your material


When When someone is staffed Always Always


What the buyer gets A reply A link, a canned answer or a form An answer, and with some agents the product itself


Qualification As good as the person on shift Fixed questions in a fixed order Through the conversation, on criteria you set


Shows the product Only by sharing a link or booking a call No Yes, if the agent can run interactive demos


Staffing Coverage for every hour you promise Someone to maintain the flows Someone to own training, rules and handoff


Cost model Mostly people Mostly software, plus upkeep time Software, often priced on usage or website traffic


## Who answers: a person, a script or an agent?


A person is still the best conversationalist on your site. A good SDR on live chat reads tone, spots a big account and knows when to stop selling.


The problem is that a person answers only the questions they are around for, and the script answers only the questions you predicted. A chatbot is a decision tree with a text box on top. It works when visitors ask what you expected, in the words you expected. B2B buyers rarely do. They ask whether you work with their stack, what a rollout looks like for a team of 40, and how you differ from the tab they have open next to yours.


An agent handles the question nobody scripted, because it answers from your docs, decks and product rather than from a flowchart. That is the real line between a chatbot and an AI agent: one returns what you wrote down, the other works out what to say from what you taught it.


## When do B2B buyers actually ask?


Often when your team isn't there.[Storylane's Modern Buying Trends 2026 report](https://www.storylane.io/buyer-experience-report) found that 51.4% of buyer conversations with website agents start outside the buyer's working hours, on weekdays and weekends (8,211 conversations across 19 companies). If that holds for your site, a live chat staffed nine to six is closed for about half of the conversations it exists to have.


Staffing more hours rarely holds up: night and weekend coverage for a handful of chats is the most expensive SDR time you can buy. The usual result is an offline form that says "we'll get back to you", which turns a live question into a ticket, and[speed to lead](https://www.storylane.io/blog/what-is-speed-to-lead) goes from minutes to the next morning. What buyers ask in those hours is in[what 1,429 off-hours buyer messages reveal](https://www.storylane.io/blog/weekend-buyer-findings) .


Chatbots and agents are both always on. The difference is in the third question.


## What does the buyer walk away with?


This is the question I would weigh most.


Live chat gives a reply, often a good one, from someone who then has to point the buyer to a page, a case study or a calendar.


A chatbot gives a link: at best a help article, often a form (and[forms asked too early suppress conversion](https://www.storylane.io/blog/why-contact-forms-suppress-conversion) ). The answers usually exist somewhere on the site. They are just far from where the buyer is standing.


The[Storylane Buyability Index](https://buyability-index.storylane.io/) shows how far. Across 10,580 buyer questions on 529 B2B websites, 41% were not fully answered by the site, and 38% of the full answers sat in the blog, help centre or developer docs rather than on the pages buyers start from. (The questions are generated per company as what a buyer would plausibly ask, not logged from real buyers.) More in[why most B2B websites answer buyer questions in the docs](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answers-hidden-in-docs) .


So a chatbot that hands out links is sending buyers on the same trip they were trying to avoid by opening the chat. I call this answer distance: the gap between where the buyer asks and where your answer lives. Live chat shortens it with a person. A chatbot rarely shortens it at all. An agent shortens it to zero by bringing the answer, and with the right agent the product, into the conversation.


Most of the buying committee never gets on a sales call: the same report puts it at nine in ten. For those people the website conversation is the demo. A buyer who asks "how does approval routing work?" and sees the approval screen learns more in a minute than one who gets a paragraph. The longer case is in[why an interactive demo plus an AI agent converts](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-demo-ai-agent-combo) .


## Which questions do buyers bring to the chat?


The ones they would rather not ask a rep. In[Storylane's Modern Buying Trends 2026 report](https://www.storylane.io/buyer-experience-report) , pricing opened 9.4% of website agent conversations against 2.5% of sales calls, and buyers were 32% more likely to raise pricing and capability with an agent than with a person. Asking a rep what something costs starts a negotiation; asking an agent costs nothing. (On whether to publish prices at all, see[should you put pricing on your website](https://www.storylane.io/blog/should-you-put-pricing-on-your-website) .)


A chatbot handles these worst, because they rarely fit a button, and live chat handles them only in office hours. Yet they decide whether a visitor books a meeting. An agent can answer them on the rules you set: what it may say about price, what it must never say about a competitor, when it should hand off. The same report found the opposite pattern for security and compliance: 1.5% of agent questions, but raised on 42% of sales calls. That is the handoff a person should own.


## Is live chat still worth it for B2B sales?


Yes, for a specific kind of site, but not as the front line for most.


### Pick live chat if


- Your deals are large and few, so every conversation justifies a person.
- Your buyers are mostly in one or two time zones and arrive during your working day.
- Your SDRs already own a chat queue short enough to answer in minutes.


### Pick a rule-based chatbot if


- Most visitors want one of a few things (support, pricing page, careers) and your job is to route them.
- You need something running this week with no training material.
- Your product is simple enough that a link genuinely answers the question.


### Pick an AI agent if


- Your buyers ask open questions about fit, setup, security and pricing, at any hour.
- Much of the buying committee will judge you from the website without ever joining a call.
- You want the website to[qualify in real time](https://www.storylane.io/blog/real-time-lead-qualification) and book, not just collect forms.


People trust people, which is why I would not pick between them. The setup that fits most B2B websites is an agent on every page, every hour, handing qualified buyers to a person with the context written down, so the person spends time on conversations worth it instead of the queue. If you are moving off a scripted bot,[what changes when you replace a chatbot with an AI sales agent](https://www.storylane.io/blog/replacing-chatbot-with-ai-sales-agent) covers the switch, and[our live chat for sales playbook](https://www.storylane.io/blog/live-chat-sales) covers running the human side well.


## What should an AI agent on a B2B website be able to do?


I work at Storylane, and we build an AI agent for websites called[Storylane RepX](https://www.storylane.io/repx) , so read this section with that in mind. These are the checks I would run on any agent, ours included.


- **It answers from your material.** RepX[trains on](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/training-repx/training-overview) your website, decks, sales call recordings or transcripts, Storylane demos and FAQs, and FAQs give a fixed answer where wording must not drift (pricing, compliance).
- **It can show the product.** RepX pulls up interactive demos in the conversation and walks the buyer through the real product. Each demo gets a[plain-language display instruction](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/training-repx/demos-images-and-videos) that controls when it appears, and RepX can also show images and videos.
- **It qualifies on your terms.** You define the ICP in plain English and the agent screens through conversation, not a form.
- **It follows rules you set once.** Guardrails on pricing, competitors and compliance, plus evaluations so you[test the agent](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/setting-up-repx/testing-your-agent) before anything goes live.
- **It changes by page.** RepX[Playbooks](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/playbooks/introduction-to-playbooks) set the starter questions, intro message, CTA buttons,[qualification questions and when to ask for an email](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/playbooks/qualification-behavior-and-goals) per page, so the pricing page books an AE and the docs page books support. More on why this matters in[page-level context for conversational AI](https://www.storylane.io/blog/page-level-context-conversational-ai) .
- **It hands off cleanly.** Qualified leads and conversation summaries flow to HubSpot, Salesforce and Slack. In[HubSpot](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/hubspot) , each conversation is logged on the contact with the full transcript and summary, and[Slack](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/slack) gets the topics, a short summary and a link to the conversation.
- **It speaks the way buyers want.** Text, voice or video (we compared the three in[text vs voice vs video conversational AI](https://www.storylane.io/blog/text-vs-voice-vs-video-conversational-ai) ).


In practice,[Hospitable booked 36 meetings and sourced 7 deals](https://www.storylane.io/customer-stories/how-hospitable-booked-36-meetings-in-a-month-with-repx) in RepX's first month. RepX starts at $2,000 a month, and the price depends on website traffic.[Chatbots vs AI agents](https://www.storylane.io/blog/chatbots-vs-ai-agents) compares those two on their own.


## The one question to ask on Monday


Open your own chat window after 7pm and ask the question your best prospect asked on their last call. Then look at what you got: a reply, a link or the product. Whatever you got is what most of your buyers get, because most of them show up when your team has gone home.


If you want to see what the product answer looks like on your own site,[book a demo of RepX](https://www.storylane.io/request-demo) .
